Examples [01–06](index.qmd) identify *teaching* plants — lumped resonances and a coupled
normal-mode expansion. This one identifies the **real thing**: a compiled
[`rtsfreerun`](https://controlsystems.docs.ligo.org/rtsfreerun) advligorts front-end model
of a LIGO HSTS suspension — *the same C filter numerics a control-room front-end runs*,
driven through the same channel API, under the digital twin's own seismic and readout noise.
No hardware; no method changes. The Pintelon–Schoukens loop (periodic multisine →
leakage-free reference FRF → maximum-likelihood fit → Cramér–Rao refinement) runs exactly as
it does on the teaching plants.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## What makes this page different
The plant here is **not** a Python lumped model — it is the compiled `x1hsts` / `x1hsts6dof`
CDS composite (built from a `.mdl` by `rtsfreerun`), carrying the as-built `HSTS_DRV_TF`
foton cascade and a 36-state MIMO suspension state space. Because that model is not installed
in CI, this page is rendered with `freeze: true` from a locally executed cache; the figures
below are real recovery runs against the compiled model, scored against an **analytic oracle**
derived from the twin's own filter definitions (`backends.rtsfreerun_oracle`).
:::

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Setup — import the presentation glue (runs the real models)"

import numpy as np
```

## A1–A2 · Open-loop SISO under the twin's own noise

The HSTS drive→sensor plant is the order-10 `HSTS_DRV_TF` cascade — **five modes** near
0.67, 1.01, 1.52, 2.81 and 3.78 Hz, each $Q\!\approx\!50$, threaded with near-cancelling
zeros. We inject the multisine at the coil-driver excitation port and read the 16-bit sensor
displacement while the twin runs `ligo-india` seismic on the ISI and BOSEM readout noise.
The FRF input is the **after-actuator drive monitor**, so the coil driver divides out and the
recovered transfer is the bare suspension. *(A1 — the wiring/oracle smoke test that gates this
page — lives in the test suite; here we go straight to recovery.)*

### What you'd watch in the control room — one raw measurement

Before any fitting, here is the raw audit: a single broadband measurement, exactly the channels
you would trend at the front end. The drive is injected through a **3 s Tukey on/off ramp**
(actuator-safe — you never slam a suspension), held at full amplitude through the measured
periods, then ramped back down; the readout is the real 16-bit sensor under the twin's seismic +
BOSEM noise. Nothing here is fitted — it is what went in and what came out.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "One raw open-loop measurement (Tukey-ramped broadband drive, twin noise)"
a2a = rd.a2_audit(seed=1)
rd.drive_response_fig(a2a)
```

You can see the drive ramp up over 3 s, the suspension ring up to steady state, and the readout
carry the modes plus the broadband sensor/seismic floor. The measurement uses only the flat
middle periods (the leakage-free, integer-period window), so the ramps fall in discarded settle.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Excitation design — the flat audit drive vs the point-optimal ASD"
rd.exc_design_fig(a2a)
```

The audit drives **flat** in-band (every line illuminated, so coherence is interpretable
everywhere); the campaign below instead spends its power budget where the Fisher information is —
the gold ASD concentrates at the five modes. Now the leakage-free reference FRF and its
**per-line coherence** — where on the band do we actually trust this measurement?

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Measured FRF vs oracle, with per-line coherence"
rd.bode_audit_fig(a2a, fit=a2a.fit)
```

Coherence sits at ~1 across the driven band (deterministic drive, modest noise); the measured FRF
(markers, with σ error bars) lands on the analytic oracle, and a quick ML fit threads it. The
**residuals** — normalised `(measured − fit)/σ` — should be a structureless ±2 scatter with a
standard-normal histogram if the noise model is right:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Normalised FRF residuals — should be ~N(0,1)"
rd.residuals_fig(a2a, a2a.fit)
```

### Optimal-excitation campaign

The audit above is a single flat sweep. The actual identification is the P&S **optimal-excitation
campaign**: a prior-robust first pass, then point-optimal refinement that concentrates the drive
where the Fisher information is, folding each pass in by inverse-variance and refitting.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Run the A2 optimal-excitation campaign against compiled x1hsts"
a2 = rd.a2_recovery(seed=1, n_passes=3)
rd.bode_overlay(a2.ff, a2.oracle, a2.fit, freq=a2.freq, H_meas=a2.H_meas,
                title="x1hsts drive→sensor — analytic oracle vs P&S recovery (noise on)")
```

The recovered model tracks the oracle through every mode and anti-resonance, and the parameter
uncertainty falls pass over pass while the peak drive stays well under the coil-driver limit.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Modal recovery + uncertainty convergence"
display(rd.modes_table(a2.oracle, a2.fit))
rd.convergence_fig(a2.fracs)
```

## A3 · Closed-loop — the real damping loops engaged

Now the `x1hsts6dof` composite: the bare-M1 **6×6 MIMO** HSTS state space with the
**production L1 `MC2_M1_DAMP` foton banks** closed around all six rigid-body DOFs
(L, T, V, R, P, Y), tuned to a $\tau\!\approx\!5$ s ringdown — the very loops that damp the
suspension in the observatory. A closed loop normally *hides* the plant: the sensor sees the
suppressed response $G/(1+GC)$, not $G$. The P&S **reference-based** estimate recovers $G$ anyway,
by taking the FRF against the **true plant input** — the drive *minus* the controller feedback
at the `COIL_DRV_SUM` junction. The feedback sign is load-bearing: negligible off-resonance,
it dominates exactly at the damped modes.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Drive each DOF open- and closed-loop; recover the plant tensor"
d = rd.a34(n_passes=2)
display(rd.diag_table(d))
```

With the loops closed, every diagonal element comes back as the **open-loop** plant to a part
in a thousand — the controller is cancelled, not fit. That is the whole point of a
reference-based closed-loop identification: you measure the suspension you want to model, not
the suppressed loop you happened to be running.

#### What the cancellation looks like in the raw time series

To see *why* it works, here is one raw closed-loop measurement on the L DoF — the four channels a
control-room audit would log: the injected `DRIVE_EXC`, the **damper feedback** it provokes, the
**reconstructed plant input** (drive − feedback, the `"+-"` `COIL_DRV_SUM` node), and the sensor
readout — all with the loops live.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "One raw closed-loop measurement — drive, damper feedback, plant input, readout"
a3a = rd.a3_audit(d, "L")
rd.loop_timeseries_fig(a3a)
```

The damper output is non-trivial (the loop is genuinely active), and the plant input is the drive
*minus* it. Taking the FRF against that reconstructed plant input — not the injected drive —
cancels the controller and returns the open-loop plant, with coherence at unity:

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Closed-loop reference FRF vs the OPEN-loop oracle, with coherence"
rd.bode_audit_fig(a3a)
```

That table is the *breadth* result — all six loops cancelled at once, nonparametrically. The
*depth* result is the **same parametric campaign as [A2](#a1a2-open-loop-siso-under-the-twins-own-noise)**,
now run through a closed loop. Taking the longitudinal (L) DoF: we seed an analytic modal prior
(its order chosen from the state-space oracle — L carries five modes; pitch and yaw carry fewer,
and over-modelling them is what used to break the optimal-excitation design), then run the
prior-robust → point-optimal refinement against the reconstructed plant input.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "A3 depth — the optimal-excitation parametric campaign, loops closed (L DoF)"
a3 = rd.a3_parametric(d, "L", n_passes=4)
rd.bode_overlay(a3.ff, a3.oracle, a3.fit, freq=a3.freq, H_meas=a3.H_meas,
                title="L drive→sense — open-loop oracle vs closed-loop parametric recovery")
```

The recovered model sits on the **open-loop** state-space oracle through all five modes — even
though the L damper (and the other five) are live. The modal parameters return to the analytic
truth, and the Cramér–Rao uncertainty falls pass over pass exactly as in the open-loop case: a
closed loop costs nothing here, because the reference-based estimate never saw it.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Closed-loop modal recovery + CRB convergence (L DoF)"
display(rd.modes_table(a3.oracle_modes, a3.fit,
                       caption="L-DoF modes — open-loop oracle vs closed-loop recovery"))
rd.convergence_fig(a3.fracs)
```

## A4 · The full 6×6 MIMO tensor

Opening the loops and driving each input DOF in turn gives the complete drive→sense FRF
tensor. The diagonals carry the suspension's anti-resonance notches; the off-diagonals are the
genuine cross-coupling — strongest on the L↔P and R↔Y pairs the suspension's geometry
dictates. Each per-pair FRF is overlaid on its analytic state-space element below (black line),
with the closed-loop diagonal recovery from A3 in green on the diagonal.

The cross-coupling is small — the diagonals peak near 18, the strongest off-diagonal near 0.15.
So the **diagonals are drawn at their true scale, and every off-diagonal element is multiplied by
one shared factor (×100)** to lift it onto the same axis (noted in the figure title and the
"oracle" legend entry). The scaling is purely for visibility; it is the same number for all 30
off-diagonal panels, so their *relative* magnitudes are preserved.

```{python}
#| code-summary: "6×6 |FRF| tensor — oracle vs open-loop (A4) and closed-loop diagonal (A3)"
rd.tensor_grid(d)
```

The off-diagonal elements *under closed loop* still carry the cross-loop bias — recovering the
coupled matrix jointly, with shared modal poles across elements, is the parametric MIMO fit
(the named Track B follow-on). The per-pair open-loop tensor here is the honest nonparametric
MIMO result, and the closed-loop diagonal is the controller-cancelled SISO recovery — both
against the same compiled twin a real front-end runs.
